summary: Lists RTCP Sender Report, Receiver Report and Extended Report metrics that may need to be supported for monitoring media streams in WebRTC, with identifiers for the WebRTC statistics API. It offers considerations for choosing which to expose.

plainLanguage.summary: Video calls can measure how well they are doing, like a doctor checking a pulse. This helps choose which measurements are worth showing to apps.

questions: rtcp xr metrics for webrtc stats
how to monitor video call quality
subtitle: Which metrics WebRTC apps should expose from RTCP and RTP monitoring

tldr.problem: WebRTC applications need to monitor the quality of media streams, but basic RTP metrics do not distinguish between different types of problems. For instance, they do not separate packets lost due to network congestion from packets discarded because they arrived too late.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8451 lists RTCP Sender Report, Receiver Report, and Extended Report metrics that applications should support. It explains why each metric helps diagnose a specific class of problem, from network issues to jitter buffer problems to repair mechanism effectiveness.
tldr.outcome: WebRTC browsers and applications can expose consistent sets of quality metrics through the WebRTC Statistics API, allowing web developers to estimate quality of experience and troubleshoot media problems.

facts.label: Basic metrics
facts.value: From RTCP SR/RR (packets sent, received, lost, jitter)

facts.label: Extended metrics
facts.value: From RTCP XR blocks (discard, burst patterns, frame impairment)

today: RFC 8451 defines the standard set of WebRTC statistics metrics. The identifiers and definitions are now part of the W3C WebRTC specification and are supported by modern browsers and WebRTC implementations. These metrics are essential for developers building adaptive media applications that respond to network conditions and for monitoring services that track call quality.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
WebRTC applications need to estimate service quality and troubleshoot media transmission. RFC 3550 defines basic RTCP Sender Report and Receiver Report metrics, such as the number of packets sent, received, and lost. However, these basic metrics provide only partial information about what happened during transmission. For example, the loss count does not distinguish between packets that were lost on the network and packets that arrived too late to be useful (discarded by the receiver's jitter buffer).

RTCP Extended Reports (XR), defined in RFC 3611 and related RFCs, provide much more detailed metrics. These include counts of discarded packets, metrics about burst loss patterns, frame-level impairment metrics for video, and information about how well error-recovery mechanisms (such as Forward Error Correction) worked. RFC 8451 identifies which of these extended metrics are most valuable for WebRTC implementations to expose through the getStats() API.
sections.plainLanguage: When a video call works, the app can count how many packets arrived, how many got lost, and how many were thrown away. Knowing the difference helps fix the problem.

sections.title: Three Categories of Metrics
sections.content:
RFC 8451 organizes metrics into three categories. Network impact metrics show what happened on the network: how many packets were lost, how many were discarded (arrived too late), and whether losses clustered together in bursts or spread out. These help diagnose network problems such as congestion or link failures. Application impact metrics show how the media quality changed at the application layer: frame-level impairments for video, jitter buffer behavior, and actual bit rates. These help estimate user experience. Recovery metrics measure how well error-recovery mechanisms worked, such as retransmission or Forward Error Correction.

Each metric type serves a different diagnostic purpose. Network metrics help identify where the problem is in the network. Application metrics help estimate what the user experiences. Recovery metrics help evaluate whether FEC or retransmission is helping or hurting throughput.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three kinds of things to measure: what the network did, how the app saw it, and whether recovery tricks helped.

sections.title: Network and Application Impact Metrics
sections.content:
Network impact metrics track packet loss and discard. The most important is distinguishing lost packets from discarded packets. A lost packet never reached the receiver because the network dropped it or a router queue overflowed. A discarded packet arrived at the receiver but was too late to play out (usually because jitter (variability in network delay) caused it to miss the playout deadline). Burst/gap loss metrics show whether losses cluster into dense bursts, because bursty loss is more damaging to perceived quality than spread-out loss. The RFC names the Gmin threshold (typically 16 packets) below which loss is considered a burst rather than occasional loss. Run-length encoding metrics represent each packet as a bit in a vector, indicating whether it was lost, discarded, repaired, or duplicated.

Application impact metrics measure quality from the user's perspective. Frame impairment metrics count full frames lost (the entire video frame is missing) versus partial frames (some packets of the frame arrived but others did not). For video, key frames (spatially compressed, no prediction from other frames) are much larger and more important than derived frames. Jitter buffer metrics show how the receiver's buffer is tuned to balance between reducing delay and accommodating network jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: When packets don't arrive, did they get lost on the network or were they too late to use? For video, some frames are more important than others. The jitter buffer is like a bucket catching packets that arrive at different speeds.

sections.title: Recovery Metrics and Measurement
sections.content:
Application impact metrics measure quality from the user's perspective. Frame impairment metrics count full frames lost (the entire video frame is missing) versus partial frames (some packets of the frame arrived but others did not). For video, key frames (spatially compressed, no prediction from other frames) are much larger and more important than derived frames (temporally compressed, depend on key frames). Losing a key frame causes more visible damage than losing a derived frame, so apps benefit from knowing which type failed. The rendered frame rate shows how many frames actually made it to the decoder without critical loss.

Jitter buffer metrics (maximum and nominal buffer size) show how the receiver's buffer is tuned. A small buffer reduces end-to-end delay but drops more late-arriving packets. A large buffer accommodates more jitter but increases delay. Knowing buffer behavior helps estimate end-user conversational quality.
sections.plainLanguage: For video, some frames are more important than others. Big key frames matter more than little update frames. The jitter buffer is like a bucket that catches packets that arrive at different speeds.

sections.title: Implementation Status
sections.content:
The metrics defined in RFC 8451 were added to the W3C WebRTC Statistics specification (webrtc-stats) during the document's development. The process for adding new metrics in the future is to create an issue or pull request on the W3C WebRTC specification repository. RTCP Extended Reports are optional in WebRTC (RFC 7841 does not mandate them), but when negotiated via SDP, implementations can send XR blocks and browsers can expose those metrics to applications.

RFC 8451 recommends that all listed identifiers be implemented by WebRTC endpoints. However, an endpoint may choose not to expose an identifier if it does not implement the corresponding RTCP report block. The document considers only RTP-layer metrics; IP-layer metrics (latency, jitter at the packet level) are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Modern web browsers now support these measurements when both sides of the call agree to send them. New measurements can be added by proposing them to the W3C.
